biblStruct.note: Daniel al-Qumisi, a ninth Century Karaite exegete, declares in two explicit statements that Scripture only has one true meaning. In the first statement, he criticizes the Rabbanites for their extensive use of non-literal interpretation (in Arabic: taʾwi1) which is connected to their belief that the Torah has 'forty-nine meanings' (an early formulation of: 'the Torah has seventy facets'). In the second statement, Qumisi states that of the two alternative interpretations that he offers, only one can be true; so too when exegetes disagree, only one interpretation can be true. In his commentary on the Twelve Minor Prophets known as Pitron Shnem Asar Qumisi appears to contradict his own explicit statements concerning the singular meaning of Scripture. Qumisi often identifies two levels of meaning: one historical and literal, relating to the era of the prophet, and the other prognostic and allegorical, relating to his own era. It appears from Qumisi's comments on the Twelve Minor Prophets and on Psalms, that he viewed these dual interpretations as two equally true levels of meaning. In his commentary on Hosea 12:11, Qumisi interprets the words 'I multiplied vision' [NJPS: 'For I granted many visions'] as God's programmatic declaration that He places several messages in a single prophecy as warnings of potential punishments both to the ancient Israelites and to the future exiles. From further evidence it is concluded that Qumisi identifies up to four levels of meaning in his interpretations: 1. a historical-literal level; 2. a historical-allegorical level; 3. a prognostic-literal level; and 4. a prognostic-allegorical level – which is not to say that every verse must have all four levels of meaning. When Qumisi identifies more than one level of meaning in a prophecy, there are usually only two levels and rarely three. Despite his criticism of the Rabbanites, Qumisi does not reject non-literal interpretation (taʾwil); on the contrary, in certain contexts it is his default mode of interpretation. Qumisi was apparently opposed to the Rabbanites' extensive use of non-literal interpretation prompted by their belief that Scripture has 'forty-nine meanings'.
